title: Warehouse Manager
statement:
A company stores its products in several warehouses:

- `Warehouse(name, product_id, units)`: one row per warehouse and product it stocks; `(name, product_id)` is unique. Warehouse `name` holds `units` units of the product, and every `product_id` exists in `Products`.
- `Products(product_id, product_name, Width, Length, Height)`: one row per product; `product_id` is unique. One unit of the product is a box of `Width * Length * Height` cubic feet.

For every warehouse that appears in `Warehouse`, find how much space its stock fills: add up, over its rows, `units` times the volume of one unit of that product.

Report the columns `warehouse_name` and `volume` (that total), one row per warehouse, in any order.
reference:
SELECT w.name AS warehouse_name,
       SUM(w.units * p.Width * p.Length * p.Height) AS volume
FROM Warehouse AS w
JOIN Products AS p
  ON p.product_id = w.product_id
GROUP BY w.name;
brute:
SELECT items.name AS warehouse_name, SUM(items.item_volume) AS volume
FROM (
  SELECT w.name,
         w.units * (
           SELECT p.Width * p.Length * p.Height
           FROM Products AS p
           WHERE p.product_id = w.product_id
         ) AS item_volume
  FROM Warehouse AS w
) AS items
GROUP BY items.name
notes:
## Intuition

The space one stock row fills is the number of units times the size of one unit, and the size lives in `Products`. Join each stock row to its product so both numbers sit on the same row, multiply, then add the results per warehouse.

## Approach

1. Read `Warehouse` (alias `w`), one row per warehouse and product.
2. `JOIN Products` (alias `p`) on `product_id` to bring in `Width`, `Length` and `Height`.
3. `GROUP BY w.name`, so each warehouse becomes one group.
4. `SUM(w.units * p.Width * p.Length * p.Height)` adds up the space of every stock row in the group, reported as `volume` next to `warehouse_name`.

## Example 1, step by step

Unit volumes: LC-TV 5 * 50 * 40 = 10000, LC-KeyChain 125, LC-Phone 200, LC-T-Shirt 800.

| warehouse | product | units | units * unit volume |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LCHouse1 | LC-TV | 1 | 10000 |
| LCHouse1 | LC-KeyChain | 10 | 1250 |
| LCHouse1 | LC-Phone | 5 | 1000 |
| LCHouse2 | LC-TV | 2 | 20000 |
| LCHouse2 | LC-KeyChain | 2 | 250 |
| LCHouse3 | LC-T-Shirt | 1 | 800 |

Summing per warehouse gives LCHouse1 12250, LCHouse2 20250 and LCHouse3 800.

## Complexity

- Time: O(W + P) for W stock rows and P products with a hash join and hash grouping.
- Space: O(P) for the join's lookup and O(number of warehouses) for the groups.

## Pitfalls

- Summing the unit volumes without multiplying by `units` counts each product once, however many units are stored.
- Grouping by `product_id` (or by both columns) reports per-product rows instead of one row per warehouse.
- The output column is `warehouse_name`, not the table's own `name`; it needs the alias.
- Products that no warehouse stocks must not create rows, so the join starts from `Warehouse`, not `Products`.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `w` | `Warehouse`, one stock row per warehouse and product |
| `p` | `Products`, the size of one unit of the stocked product |
| `warehouse_name` | the warehouse's `name`, the grouping key |
| `volume` | total cubic feet of all units in that warehouse |

narration.1: Each output row names a warehouse.
narration.2: Space of one stock row is units times the unit box volume; summing gives the warehouse total.
narration.3: Start from the stock rows, so only warehouses that hold something appear.
narration.4: Join each stock row to its product to get its dimensions.
narration.6: One group per warehouse collects all of its stock rows.
